items.q: At Meta, what determines whether your design round is System Design or Product Architecture?

options.t: A role tag chosen when you apply, weeks before the interview
options.why: Right — and that's why it matters so much. The fork happens at application time, so you must choose your exam (and start prepping for it) before the loop is even scheduled.

options.t: The interviewer picks on the day based on your resume
options.why: No — the track is fixed in advance by the role you applied to. Discovering the fork on interview day is exactly the mistake this chapter exists to prevent.

options.t: You choose at the start of the interview
options.why: There's no on-the-spot menu. By interview day the round type is already set; your only choice point was the application.

options.t: E5 candidates always get System Design; E4 gets Product Architecture
options.why: The fork is by role flavor, not by level. Both tracks exist at E5 — Product Architecture is not a junior variant, it's a different exam with its own hard parts.

items.q: Which set of concerns does Meta's Product Architecture round grade that System Design barely touches?

options.t: Client-server interaction, API design, data model, live updates
options.why: Yes. PA is the user-product exam: what travels over the wire, pagination and idempotency in the API, the entities behind the product, and how a new message reaches a phone in under a second.

options.t: Distributed queues, cache hierarchies, and web-crawler politeness
options.why: That's the System Design track — backend machinery with no UI. PA problems have users and clients in the frame.

options.t: UI layout and visual design
options.why: Tempting because 'product' sounds like pixels, but PA grades the architecture behind the product — the client-server contract — not what the screen looks like.

options.t: Coding speed on product features
options.why: Coding is graded in separate rounds. PA is still a whiteboard design conversation; it just centers on a user-facing product's architecture.

items.q: You interview for Meta E5: coding rounds strong, behavioral strong, design round complete but shallow. The most commonly reported outcome is:

options.t: An offer — at E4
options.why: Right. Meta's design round is the leveler. A shallow-but-complete design performance typically down-levels you rather than rejecting you — which is why the round carries level, scope, and money on its back.

options.t: A rejection
options.why: Usually not — Meta tends to down-level strong candidates with weak design rounds rather than reject them. The E4 offer is the classic outcome, and for many candidates it stings more.

options.t: An E5 offer, since the other rounds carry it
options.why: The other rounds can't carry the level. E5 requires the design round to show depth (the technical-excellence competency); without it, the committee lands on E4.

options.t: A repeat of just the design round
options.why: Follow-up rounds happen occasionally, but they're not the norm and not something to plan around. Plan for one round deciding your level, because that's the standard shape.

items.q: Meta grades four design competencies. Which one specifically requires 'real depth in at least one area' at E5?

options.t: Technical excellence
options.why: Yes. At E5, technical excellence means breadth plus at least one component where you clearly know more than the diagram shows. Plan before the interview which component you'll take deep.

options.t: Problem navigation
options.why: Problem navigation is about scoping the vague prompt and finding the hard part — essential, but it's the breadth-and-judgment axis, not the depth axis.

options.t: Solution design
options.why: Solution design grades whether the overall architecture is complete and reasonable. You can score well here and still fail the depth bar — that's the classic E4 outcome.

options.t: Communication
options.why: Communication grades whether the interviewer can follow you without effort. It amplifies the other competencies but doesn't substitute for depth.

items.q: In the typical Google L5 design round pacing, which phase gets the most time?

options.t: The deep dive — roughly 25 of 45 minutes
options.why: Right. The Google shape is ~3 minutes requirements, ~10 high-level, ~25 deep dive, ~7 trade-offs. More than half the interview is depth — and the deep dive is explicitly what separates L5 from L4.

options.t: Requirements gathering — you can't design what you haven't scoped
options.why: Scoping matters, but Google prompts are already narrow slices ('Docs commenting'), so ~3 minutes suffices. Spending 15 minutes on requirements starves the phase that decides the level.

options.t: The high-level design — the complete picture is what's graded
options.why: The complete picture qualifies you (about 10 minutes); it doesn't level you. An L4 answer spends the remaining time widening; an L5 answer digs.

options.t: Trade-off discussion at the end
options.why: Trade-offs get about 7 minutes of explicit wrap-up — though good candidates weave them throughout. It's the deep dive that owns the clock.

items.q: What does NALSD (Non-Abstract Large System Design) demand that a normal design answer might skip?

options.t: Arithmetic at every scaling step — QPS, IOPS, machine counts
options.why: Exactly. NALSD's one-sentence idea: a design isn't real until it has numbers on it. 'Add a caching layer' fails; 'a 40 GB hot set, so it fits in RAM on one machine, replicated three times' passes.

options.t: Knowledge of Google-internal technologies like Spanner and Borg
options.why: No internal tech knowledge is expected — the method works with generic disks, RAM, and machines. What's demanded is arithmetic, not vocabulary.

options.t: Designing for at least a billion users
options.why: NALSD starts small on purpose — design for one machine first, then scale up with math. The discipline is in the arithmetic of each step, not in the size of the final number.

options.t: A formal written design document
options.why: It's still a whiteboard conversation. 'Non-abstract' refers to the content — no hand-wavy boxes — not the format.

items.q: Palantir's decomp round primarily grades:

options.t: Requirements discovery, stakeholders, data modeling, v1 prioritization
options.why: Yes — everything that happens before architecture. The prompt is a vague operational problem ('track infection spread'), and the grade rides on whether you find the real problem, the real users, and the smallest useful first version.

options.t: Distributed-systems architecture and how it survives at scale
options.why: Scale barely features. The prompts often aren't even explicitly software problems — reaching for load balancers on an undefined problem is the round's signature failure.

options.t: Graph algorithms, since the problems involve networks
options.why: This is the trap that eats strong algorithmists: the infection prompt looks like a graph problem, but an elegant traversal on data nobody defined, entered by nurses days late, solves nothing. The algorithm is never what's graded.

options.t: Prior domain knowledge of fields like healthcare or aviation
options.why: No domain expertise is expected — the domains rotate precisely so nobody has it. What's graded is how you discover a domain you don't know: by asking who does what, with which data, deciding what.

items.q: Anthropic's 90-minute coding screen is best described as:

options.t: A practical build against a spec that keeps extending
options.why: Right. It's explicitly not LeetCode: you implement a small working system, then the spec keeps stacking requirements. Ship part one fast and clean enough to survive parts two through four.

options.t: Two hard LeetCode problems under time pressure
options.why: The opposite — candidates who prepped with algorithm grinding consistently report running out of time. There are no DP riddles; the grade is on working, extendable code.

options.t: A take-home project you complete on your own time and submit for review
options.why: It's live and timed (CodeSignal-style, in-browser), which is exactly why speed matters. A take-home rewards polish; this screen rewards velocity plus structure.

options.t: A systems trivia quiz about LLMs
options.why: LLM-serving knowledge belongs to the onsite design round, not the screen. The screen is hands-on-keyboard building.

items.q: TTFT (time to first token) measures:

options.t: The delay from sending a request until the first piece of the response appears
options.why: Yes — and it's the latency users actually feel. A reply can stream for 20 seconds without complaint as long as it starts in under one. That's why LLM serving obsesses over TTFT rather than total response time.

options.t: The total time to generate the complete response, first token to last
options.why: That's end-to-end generation time, and users tolerate a lot of it — because they're reading as it streams. The felt latency is the silence before the first word, which is what TTFT captures.

options.t: How many tokens per second the model produces once the response starts streaming
options.why: That's throughput (tokens/sec), a different metric. TTFT is a latency: one duration per request, not a rate.

options.t: The time to tokenize the input prompt
options.why: Tokenization is a tiny slice of it. TTFT covers everything before output begins — queueing for a batch slot, processing the whole prompt — and queueing is usually the part that blows up under load.

items.q: Profile: 6 years on data pipelines, Kafka, and a sharded MySQL fleet; two GraphQL side projects; heavy Instagram user. Applying to Meta E5 — which design track, and why?

options.t: System Design — her production depth lives on the backend, and E5 requires one genuinely deep area
options.why: Right. The technical-excellence competency wants at least one area where she can deep-dive from experience. Pipelines and sharding are exactly that terrain; on Product Architecture her depth evaporates.

options.t: Product Architecture — years of daily Instagram use mean she knows the product inside out
options.why: Familiarity as a user is worth nothing; PA grades the parts users never see — pagination contracts, reconnect logic, client failure handling. Picking the 'familiar-feeling' exam over the deep one is the classic fork mistake.

options.t: Product Architecture — the GraphQL side projects prove she can hold her own on real-world API design
options.why: Two side projects give breadth, not depth — and depth is what decides E5 versus E4. When the interviewer drills three levels down into live updates, side-project knowledge runs out on level one.

options.t: Either — the four competencies are the same in both rounds
options.why: The rubric is the same; her ability to score on it is not. The track choice determines whether the hardest question lands on her strongest ground or her weakest — that's not a coin flip.

items.q: Mid-round at Meta, you've already resharded once after a '10x users' push. The interviewer says: 'Great. Now 100x again.' What should you understand about this moment?

options.t: This is the format working as designed — iterate calmly again, naming what breaks first
options.why: Yes. Meta rounds deliberately break your design repeatedly — candidates report redesigning sharding two and three times in one interview. The grade is on how you evolve a breaking design, so a second push means you're getting the real exam.

options.t: Your first resharding was wrong, and they're giving you a chance to fix it
options.why: Not necessarily wrong at all — designs that were right at 10x legitimately break at 100x. Reading every push as criticism makes candidates defensive, which is the actual failure mode.

options.t: They've run out of prepared material and are improvising to fill time
options.why: The 100x push IS the prepared question. Iteration under scale pressure is the core of the Meta design round, not filler.

options.t: You should defend the current design — a well-built sharding scheme should already handle 100x
options.why: Almost no design survives a genuine 100x untouched, and claiming yours does reads as either not understanding your own bottlenecks or stonewalling the exam. Find what breaks and evolve it.

items.q: Google round, minute 14. Your high-level design is complete. The interviewer has been nearly silent, occasionally taking notes. Your move:

options.t: Tell them: 'the hard part is comment-anchoring under concurrent edits — that's where I'll spend our time' — and dig
options.why: Right. Google's format is candidate-driven, and the ~25-minute deep dive is where L5 is decided. Silence is the format, not a verdict — the interviewer is waiting to see whether you drive.

options.t: Ask the interviewer what they'd like to explore next
options.why: This hands back the exact signal being measured. At Google, waiting to be led is itself the L4 marker — the quiet interviewer is quiet on purpose.

options.t: Keep adding breadth — CDN, monitoring, multi-region, backups — until the interviewer visibly reacts
options.why: Widening instead of digging is the textbook L4 pattern. The level lives at the floor of two or three components, not at the edges of the diagram.

options.t: Pause and wait — their silence suggests something's wrong
options.why: Misreading Google's silence as disapproval makes candidates flail. Note-taking silence is normal; the only wrong response to it is stopping.

items.q: Google interviewer: 'You sharded the index. How many machines?' Your service does 200K QPS; one server handles ~8K QPS. The NALSD-passing answer is:

options.t: '200K over 8K is 25 machines; call it 40 with headroom and replication — and next I'd check memory per shard'
options.why: Division out loud, a provisioning judgment on top, and the next binding constraint named — that's non-abstract. The number isn't the end; it's a step that surfaces the next question.

options.t: 'We'd run it on an autoscaling group, so the exact machine count doesn't matter — it flexes with load'
options.why: Autoscaling is a mechanism for varying the count, not an excuse to not know it. NALSD exists precisely to catch this deflection — you still must know what one machine handles and what resource runs out first.

options.t: 'Probably a few dozen, depending on the hardware'
options.why: The hedge gives away that no arithmetic happened. You have both numbers — 200K and 8K — and refusing to divide them is the hand-wavy-box behavior the round is designed to detect.

options.t: 'I'd want to benchmark a real server before committing to any specific number'
options.why: Right instinct for production, wrong move at the whiteboard. The interview gives you planning figures so you can reason with them; deferring to a benchmark you can't run is a dodge, not rigor.

items.q: In a Google round you're choosing between single-region and multi-region deployment for a read-heavy service. The most Google-calibrated way to decide:

options.t: Ask what availability SLO we're promising — 99.9% permits single-region; 99.99% forces redundancy and failover
options.why: This is the SLO-as-arbiter move: 99.99% is under an hour of downtime a year, which buys multi-zone redundancy and automated failover with a number instead of taste. Google-calibrated candidates spend from the SLO like a budget.

options.t: Multi-region from day one — it's Google, so assume the highest availability tier is required
options.why: Assuming maximal requirements is over-engineering with a famous logo on it. Multi-region costs real complexity (data replication, failover, consistency), and buying it without a target that demands it reads as unjustified complexity.

options.t: Single-region to start — it's dramatically simpler, and you can always add regions later if needed
options.why: Simplicity-by-default is healthy, but committing before knowing the availability target is deciding blind. The senior move is extracting the requirement that makes this decision for you.

options.t: Whichever the interviewer seems to prefer
options.why: Reading the interviewer instead of the requirements is the waiting-to-be-led pattern. Google's quiet-interviewer format gives you almost no signal to read anyway — the SLO is the signal.

items.q: Palantir decomp prompt: 'An infection is spreading through a city. Help us track it.' Your best first ten minutes:

options.t: Ask who uses this and what they decide with it — who enters the data, and how fresh it actually is
options.why: Right. The round grades discovery before design. These questions surface the real constraints — nurses entering contacts by hand mid-crisis, days-stale data — that make or break everything you build afterward.

options.t: Model the contact network as a graph and outline a cluster-detection algorithm
options.why: The signature failure. It's technically sound and solves a problem nobody defined — precise answers to outdated questions if the data is stale and hand-entered. The round exists to catch exactly this reflex.

options.t: Sketch the high-level architecture: ingestion, database, an API, dashboards per user type
options.why: Architecture before discovery is the same mistake in ops clothing. Boxes and arrows for undefined requirements is what the cold-open candidate did — the interviewer's 'who looks at this?' question is waiting.

options.t: Estimate the data volume — cases per day, contacts per case — to size the system
options.why: Estimation is a great habit in scale-focused rounds, but here it sizes a system you haven't justified building. The volumes are tiny anyway; the hard questions are who, what for, and what first — not how big.

items.q: In Palantir's FDSE skeptical-client pitch, your prototype (built on their messy data) has a real limitation the 'client' zeroes in on. The graded response is:

options.t: Acknowledge the limit plainly, show what the prototype does deliver, and say what closing the gap takes
options.why: The round grades honest communication under pushback — the actual FDSE job is defending work to skeptical customers without overselling. Composure plus candor plus a path forward is the full score.

options.t: Minimize it — 'that's an edge case that rarely matters in practice'
options.why: The skeptic is scripted to push, and minimizing invites the follow-up that unravels you. A client who catches you soft-pedaling once stops trusting everything else you claim — which is the exact dynamic being tested.

options.t: Pivot to the prototype's strengths and demo another feature
options.why: A visible dodge. The interviewer raised the limitation to watch you engage with it; redirecting reads as evasion, and evasion under client pressure is disqualifying for a role that lives on client trust.

options.t: Walk through the technical reasons their messy data made that part impossible in the time given
options.why: True, perhaps — but blaming the data to a client whose data it is fails the room. FDSEs succeed in messy reality; the graded skill is owning constraints, not litigating them.

items.q: Designing a Claude-style chat service in an Anthropic round: what usually caps how many concurrent conversations one GPU can serve?

options.t: GPU memory — each conversation's KV cache grows with context length and must stay resident
options.why: Yes — the number-one surprise for newcomers. The KV cache (stored attention state, kept so each new token doesn't recompute the whole context) eats GPU memory per conversation, and long contexts eat it fast. Memory runs out before compute does.

options.t: GPU compute — every generated token costs a full forward pass through billions of weights
options.why: Compute matters for throughput, but it's rarely the binding constraint on concurrency. The restaurant analogy: the kitchen could cook for a hundred diners — it's the tables (memory) that run out.

options.t: Network bandwidth streaming tokens to clients
options.why: Token streams are tiny — a few dozen bytes per token per conversation. Network is orders of magnitude away from being the bottleneck here.

options.t: Disk I/O for loading model weights per request
options.why: Weights load once and stay resident in GPU memory across all requests — they're never reloaded per request. The per-conversation cost is the KV cache, which is exactly the point.

items.q: Your LLM API limits orgs to 60 requests/minute. One org sends 60 requests of ~100K tokens each and stays compliant while your p99 TTFT collapses for everyone. The fix:

options.t: Switch the limit to tokens per minute per org, debited as tokens are consumed
options.why: Right. Cost and GPU time are proportional to tokens, not requests — a 100K-token request costs ~1000x a 100-token one, and a request-based limiter is blind to the difference. In practice: debit prompt tokens plus the max_tokens cap at admission, settle after generation.

options.t: Lower the limit to 20 requests/minute
options.why: Punishes every light user while the heavy org still pushes ~2M tokens/minute through. Tightening a limiter that measures the wrong quantity can't fix it — it's the metric that's broken, not the threshold.

options.t: Provision more GPUs so the fleet has enough headroom to absorb the heavy org's load without queueing
options.why: Buys time at enormous cost and leaves the design flaw intact — the next heavy org saturates the bigger fleet just as compliantly. In a round graded on cost, 'add GPUs' to dodge a rate-limiter design flaw is the worst possible look.

options.t: Reject requests over 10K tokens
options.why: A crude cap that breaks legitimate long-context use — the very feature users pay for — while still letting someone send 60 near-cap requests a minute. Budgeting tokens serves both goals; banning length serves neither.

items.q: Meta Product Architecture round, designing Messenger. Interviewer: 'How do new messages reach the recipient's phone?' Which answer reads E5?

options.t: 'Persistent WebSocket, because sub-second delivery is the product — long-polling fallback, and sequence numbers so a reconnecting client catches up.'
options.why: Commitment, a reason tied to the product requirement, a fallback for the real-world failure case, and the reconnect story — client-server depth is exactly what PA grades, and the sequence-number detail shows you've thought past the happy path.

options.t: 'There are several options — push notifications, periodic polling, or WebSockets — and each has trade-offs depending on the requirements'
options.why: Option-listing with no decision. The requirement is sitting right there (it's a messenger; delivery must feel instant), so 'depending on requirements' signals you didn't use the requirements you have.

options.t: 'The client polls every 5 seconds — it's simpler, stateless, and works through any proxy'
options.why: A commitment, credit for that — but it fails the product: multi-second delivery lag in a chat app, plus a stampede of empty polls from millions of idle clients. Simplicity that breaks the core requirement isn't senior restraint, it's a missed requirement.

options.t: 'Kafka streams the messages directly to each client'
options.why: Kafka is a server-side log for services, not a delivery channel to phones — clients don't hold Kafka consumer connections. This is buzzword architecture: a real technology deployed where it doesn't fit, which reads worse than a plain answer.

items.q: Google round: a candidate delivers a flawless, complete design of Docs commenting — every component sensible — then spends the back half adding breadth (CDN, monitoring, multi-region) and answering follow-ups well. The likely grade and why:

options.t: L4 — complete and competent, but nobody ever saw the floor of any component
options.why: This is the L4/L5 line in one sentence: breadth qualifies, depth levels. L5 required spending the 25-minute middle digging into one hard problem with concrete numbers, unprompted — and 'answered follow-ups well' means the interviewer drove, which at Google is itself part of the grade.

options.t: L5 — the design was complete and every answer was correct
options.why: Correct-and-complete is the L4 bar. The L5 signal — self-directed depth with arithmetic — never appeared, and no amount of correct breadth substitutes for it.

options.t: L5 — breadth across CDN, monitoring, and multi-region shows range
options.why: Widening is what candidates do when they don't know where to dig. Range across shallow coverage is precisely the pattern Google's format is built to distinguish from depth — it reads as the opposite of what it hopes to.

options.t: Impossible to say — design grading is subjective and depends on the interviewer you draw
options.why: There's calibration noise at the margins, but this pattern isn't marginal: Google trains interviewers on the depth-separates-levels rubric specifically. Complete-plus-shallow lands on L4 with high consistency — that predictability is why the pacing advice exists.

items.q: Anthropic round, LLM inference API. You must set the continuous-batching batch size. Bigger batches raise GPU utilization (cheaper per token) but slow every request's token steps. The strongest answer:

options.t: 'Set a p99 TTFT budget — say one second — then size the batch cap to the largest value that holds it, naming the utilization we give up'
options.why: Commit-and-justify with the trade-off priced: a latency target as the constraint, batch size derived from it, and the cost of the choice named out loud. If finance pushes back later, the knob and its price are explicit — exactly the cost-versus-percentiles judgment this round grades.

options.t: 'Maximize batch size — GPU cost dominates, so utilization wins'
options.why: Optimizing one axis to the wall while silently sacrificing p99 TTFT — the metric users feel — is happy-path cost thinking. The interviewer's next question ('what happened to your tail latency?') dismantles it in one move.

options.t: 'Keep batches at one request per GPU so latency is always optimal'
options.why: This can inflate cost enormously — modern serving gets much of its throughput from batching. Buying perfect latency at that multiple, unexamined, fails the cost axis as badly as the previous option fails latency.

options.t: 'Make it a config knob, ship a reasonable default, and tune it in production against real traffic instead of guessing at a whiteboard'
options.why: It will be configurable — but 'tune later' at the whiteboard is deferring the exact reasoning being examined. The question is what the knob trades against what, and picking a defensible starting point is the demonstration of judgment.

items.q: Palantir decomp, gate-assignment prompt. One candidate designs an elegant constraint-solver that computes optimal gate assignments. Another proposes 'a live board showing current assignments with conflicts highlighted the moment a delay lands.' Who scores higher, and why?

options.t: The live board — a v1 that helps a real stakeholder tomorrow, built on what controllers actually lack
options.why: The round grades discovery and prioritization, not technical ambition. The board answer implies the candidate asked who decides and what they lack; the solver answer implies they pattern-matched 'scheduling → optimization' and skipped the humans. Shipping visibility before automation is the classic right call in operational software.

options.t: The solver — it actually removes the chaos by computing good assignments instead of just displaying the problem
options.why: It solves a formalization of the problem — one nobody validated. Optimal assignments from a solver controllers don't trust (and will override on day one, using knowledge the model lacks) help less than making the conflict visible ten minutes sooner. 'More technology' is not the round's scoring axis.

options.t: The solver, provided it handles the constraints correctly
options.why: Correctness of the solver was never the doubt — that's the point. A flawless answer to an undefined problem is the decomp round's signature failure; the retold infection-tracking disasters are exactly this pattern with different nouns.

options.t: Both equal — one is v1 and the other is v2 of the same system
options.why: There's a real roadmap where the board precedes the solver — but the round grades which one you build first and why. Leading with v2 demonstrates the priority inversion; the sequencing IS the assessment, not a detail of it.

items.q: Anthropic round: your design serves search over 1B documents, sharded 100 ways, every query fanning out to all shards. It works at 1K QPS. At 10K QPS, what degrades first, and what's the strong answer?

options.t: Tail latency — every query waits for its slowest shard; mitigate with replicas plus hedged requests
options.why: Fan-out tail amplification is the real mechanism: with 100 shards per query, one slow shard in a hundred makes nearly every query slow. Naming the failure, the standard mitigations (replication, hedging — sending a backup request when the first is slow), and their price is the graded pattern.

options.t: Nothing structural — add 10x machines and throughput follows
options.why: More replicas do buy throughput, but the tail problem worsens independently: fan-out width hasn't changed, so every query still samples 100 shards' worst moments. Scaling capacity without addressing tail mechanics is the 'horizontally scalable' incantation this round is designed to push through.

options.t: Shard the index 1000 ways instead of 100
options.why: Backwards for the tail: wider fan-out samples more shards per query, making the p99 worse, not better. This is the trap of treating sharding as a universal scale answer without tracing what the query path actually does.

options.t: Put a result cache in front — popular queries stop fanning out at all, and the problem mostly disappears
options.why: A result cache genuinely helps repeated queries and belongs in the design — but search traffic has a long tail of unique queries the cache never sees, and those still fan out 100 ways. Offering caching as the complete answer ducks the mechanism the question is probing.

items.q: You have Google and Meta onsites two weeks apart and ten evenings of prep. A friend says 'system design is system design — just do mocks.' The senior-calibrated plan:

options.t: Split by exam: numbers-to-reflex drills and '100x' mocks for Meta; timed 25-minute solo deep dives with machine math for Google
options.why: The two rounds test different muscles to failure — Meta tests iteration speed with numbers on tap; Google tests self-driven depth with arithmetic. Generic mocks train neither edge, and the edges are where each company's level decision lives.

options.t: The friend is right — the fundamentals transfer across companies, so run as many general mocks as the evenings allow
options.why: Fundamentals do transfer — that's chapter 1 — but the failure modes don't: candidates fail Meta rounds by iterating slowly with strong fundamentals, and Google rounds by staying shallow with strong fundamentals. Prep aimed at nothing hits neither exam's edge.

options.t: Spend all ten evenings on Google — it's the harder interview
options.why: 'Harder' isn't a property of the company; it's a property of the mismatch with your reflexes. And abandoning Meta prep means walking into the round that decides E5-versus-E4 — one round, level on the line — cold. Both stakes are real.

options.t: Use the evenings to memorize five more classic architectures — feed, chat, crawler, ride-sharing, Dropbox
options.why: Architecture memorization is breadth prep, and neither company's senior bar is failed on breadth. Meta breaks your memorized design in minute ten with a 100x push; Google asks for the math your memorized diagram doesn't contain. Reflexes beat recall in both rooms.

items.q: In Anthropic's values round you're asked how you think about AI risk. You have genuine, somewhat uncertain views. The strongest approach:

options.t: Give your actual considered view, including where you're uncertain and what shifted your thinking
options.why: The round detects borrowed opinions; genuine engagement with real uncertainty reads as exactly the kind of thinking a safety-focused company wants in the building. Articulate does not mean certain — it means you've actually thought.

options.t: Recite the strongest safety-forward position you've read — this is a safety company, match the message
options.why: Rehearsed slogans are the named failure mode: interviewers probe one level down ('what would change your mind?') and borrowed positions have no foundations under them. Detected performance costs more than honest disagreement would.

options.t: Stay neutral — technical roles shouldn't require opinions on this
options.why: At most companies, fine. At Anthropic the values round is a real, graded part of the loop precisely because the mission is the company — declining to engage with it answers the question, just not in your favor.

options.t: Keep it brief and steer back to technical topics where you're strong
options.why: The steer is visible, and it treats the round as an obstacle rather than an interview — in a loop where this round is weighted like the others. Spending real prep time forming views is the fix; dodging on the day is not.
